keyTakeaways: English "sister-in-law" covers four separate Indian relations — nanad, jethani, devrani and bhabhi — and the four do not share a register.

A full-text search of Platts' 1884 Urdu and Classical Hindi dictionary returns 20 entries containing "sister-in-law", and McGregor's 1993 Oxford Hindi-English Dictionary returns 9; neither uses the phrase for jethani or devrani.
Jethani and devrani are built from jeth and devar plus the wife-of suffix -ani, so her seniority comes from her husband's birth order rather than her own age.
The term you use about her is not the term you call her: write Jiji, Didi or her name, which McGregor marks as a vocative form, not nanad or jethani.
Aim for one line — the median personal message across 197 SubhSandesh birthday pages is 96 characters, and 50.0% of the 182 dated pages were created on the birthday itself.

faqs.question: How do I wish my sister-in-law a happy birthday?
faqs.answer: Decide which sister-in-law she is first, because the four Indian relations English calls sister-in-law take different registers. For your husband's elder brother's wife use the honour register and address her as Jiji; for his younger brother's wife use her name and be warmer; for your husband's sister use Didi if she is older. Then keep it to about 96 characters.

faqs.question: What is the difference between nanad, jethani, devrani and bhabhi?
faqs.answer: Nanad is your husband's sister. Jethani is your husband's elder brother's wife. Devrani is your husband's younger brother's wife. Bhabhi is your own brother's wife. English calls all four sister-in-law because its terminology sets the spouse of a sibling equal to the sibling of a spouse.

faqs.question: What should I actually call my sister-in-law in a birthday message?
faqs.answer: Not the relationship term. Nanad, jethani and devrani are words you use about her to a third person, not words you call her. The Oxford Hindi-English Dictionary marks jiji as a vocative form of address used by women to a senior lady, so Jiji, Didi or simply her name are the natural choices.

faqs.question: Is my jethani senior to me even if she is younger?
faqs.answer: Yes. Jethani is formed from jeth, husband's elder brother, plus the suffix -ani that builds wife-of terms from nouns of status. Her standing comes from her husband's birth order, not her own age, so a jethani who is younger in years still takes the more formal register.

faqs.question: Can I call my husband's elder brother's wife bhabhi?
faqs.answer: Many families do, and it will not offend anyone. It is worth knowing that the dictionaries reserve bhabhi for a brother's wife, and McGregor narrows it further to an elder brother's wife. If you want the precise term for your husband's elder brother's wife, that is jethani, and the address form is Jiji.

faqs.question: What is a good short birthday message for a sister-in-law?
faqs.answer: One line does the job. "Happy birthday, Jiji. You made this house easy to walk into. Wishing you a wonderful year." is 89 characters, comfortably inside the 96-character median measured across 197 SubhSandesh birthday pages. Add a photograph rather than a second paragraph.

faqs.question: Should the wish be in Hindi or in English?
faqs.answer: English carries the sentence and Hindi carries the address form, which is how most Indian families already write. Keep the greeting and the message in English and use the kinship address term — Jiji, Didi, Bhabhi — where a name would otherwise go. That reads natural rather than translated.

faqs.question: How formal should I be with my devrani?
faqs.answer: Less formal than with anyone else on the list. The Bhojpuri data records women using the neutral-level interjection for a husband's younger brother's wife and the honour-level one for his elder brother's wife. Warmth is expected with a devrani; teasing is usually fine if you are close.

faqs.question: Is there a form of address I should avoid completely?
faqs.answer: Yes. The Bhojpuri study reports that the intimacy-level particle re, used by a wife toward her husband's siblings or his family, is regarded as highly impolite. Whatever else you do, do not reach for the most casual register with in-laws unless they use it with you first.

faqs.question: I missed my sister-in-law's birthday. What do I send now?
faqs.answer: Something that admits it in the first clause. About 12.6% of the 182 dated SubhSandesh birthday pages were created after the birthday had already passed, so you are in ordinary company. "A day late, Jiji, and no excuse" beats a message written as though it arrived on time.

faqs.question: Should I add a quiz or a game to a birthday page for my sister-in-law?
faqs.answer: Usually not. A quiz was built on 98.5% of SubhSandesh birthday pages and played on only 14.4% of them. The message and the photographs are what get read, so spend the twenty minutes on the line you address her by rather than on interactive extras nobody opens.

faqs.question: Does the same wish work for all my sisters-in-law?
faqs.answer: No, and that is the main thing this page argues. The register differs by relation and by whose birth order sets her rank, so a line that reads affectionately to a devrani can read impertinent to a jethani. Write one line each and change the address form.

article.contentMarkdown:
# Birthday Wishes for Sister in Law: Four Relations, One Word

Birthday wishes for sister in law only work once you settle which sister-in-law she is. English gives you one term; a north Indian family runs four — *nanad* (your husband's sister), *jethani* (your husband's elder brother's wife), *devrani* (your husband's younger brother's wife) and *bhabhi* (your brother's wife). They do not take the same register, and two of them are ranked against each other.

Keep it short, and write it today. The median personal message across 197 birthday pages built on SubhSandesh is **96 characters**. Of 182 pages carrying a recorded birthday date, **91 — exactly 50.0% — were created on the birthday itself**, and 12.6% after it had already passed.

Below: the two dictionaries, the address forms, and one wish per relation.

## Four relations, one English term

English does not blur these by accident. It does it by rule.

A formal analysis of American kinship terminology published in *Ethnology* in 2007 generates the whole terminology from a handful of structural equations. Equation (5), which the author calls the ["Sibling-in-law" equation](https://escholarship.org/uc/item/93c7072g), reads: *Spouse of Child of Parent = Child of Parent of Spouse*.

Read it slowly: the spouse of my sibling equals the sibling of my spouse. Your brother's wife and your husband's sister are set equal by the grammar of the terminology, not because anyone thinks they are alike.

The paper adds that this logic "is not overtly known to users" who nonetheless apply it without error. The vagueness in this phrase is not yours. It is in the word.

Hindi declines that equation, keeps four terms, and adds a distinction English has no machinery for at all: which of your husband's brothers she married. The brother's wife already has her own page here, so the three covered properly below are nanad, jethani and devrani.

## What two dictionaries will not call a sister-in-law

Searching the full text of Platts' 1884 [*Dictionary of Urdu, Classical Hindi, and English*](https://dsal.uchicago.edu/cgi-bin/app/platts_query.py?qs=sister-in-law) for the string "sister-in-law" on 27 August 2026 returns **20 entries**. The same search in McGregor's 1993 [*Oxford Hindi-English Dictionary*](https://dsal.uchicago.edu/cgi-bin/app/mcgregor_query.py?qs=sister-in-law) returns **9**.

Neither spends it on jethani or devrani. Platts glosses *jeṭhānī* as "the wife of a husband's elder brother" and *dewrānī* as "husband's younger brother's wife" — descriptions of the route through the family, because there is no English word to reach for.

McGregor gets to English only by bolting on a modifier: under its entry for the suffix *-ānī* it renders devrānī as "junior sister-in-law". Junior to whom is precisely the question, and the answer is not her age.

The two also disagree about bhabhi: Platts gives "brother's wife", McGregor narrows it to "**elder** brother's wife".

## The word you use about her is not the word you call her

Kin terms do two separate jobs, and both dictionaries mark the difference on the page.

Platts' entry for *nanad* stops to explain that a woman avoids the word "husband", "whether in addressing or speaking of her partner", using *nand-kā bhāʼī*, "sister-in-law's brother", instead. McGregor, 109 years later, tags that same substitute as an "auspicious form of **reference** on a wife's part".

Reference is what you use to a third party: *she is my jethani*. Address is what goes on the card. Almost nobody writes "Happy birthday, Nanad ji": the term describes the relation, it does not hail her.

The address forms are a smaller set, and the dictionaries tag those too.

McGregor's entry for *jījī* gives sense 1 as "an elder sister-in-law" and sense 2 as a "**voc.** form of address to a senior lady", noted as women's usage. Platts lists *bībī-jī* twice inside one entry — as a noun, "husband's sister, sister-in-law", and as an **intj.**: "(A respectful form of address), Lady! Madam!"

That is the practical lesson. Write Jiji, Didi, or her name. Never the reference term.

## Her seniority is her husband's, not her own

Here is the point the listicles cannot reach, and the morphology proves it.

McGregor's entry for the suffix *-ānī* says it "forms feminines for m. nouns expressing occupation or status", and gives *kṣatrāṇī*, "wife of a kṣatriya", in the same breath as devrānī.

*Jethani* is *jeth* plus that suffix; *devrani* is *devar* plus that suffix. Jeth means "eldest, senior" and, as a noun, "a husband's elder brother"; devar is "husband's younger brother".

Her term derives from his. A jethani can be five years younger than you and still senior; a devrani can be a decade older and still junior. You cannot read the register off her age — exactly the mistake an English wishes list invites.

This is not a Hindi eccentricity. A 2014 paper on the componential analysis of kin terms in the *Journal of Universal Language* lists ["seniority within one generation"](http://www.sejongjul.org/download/download_pdf?pid=jul-15-1-129), elder against younger, and "affinity of the last connecting relative", consanguineal against affinal, among the dimensions known since Kroeber in 1909 to be used universally in the world's kinship vocabularies. English has both and declines to use either here.

## What people actually say out loud

The closest measured evidence comes from Bhojpuri, spoken across the eastern Hindi belt. A study of [vocative interjections and honorifics](https://pressto.amu.edu.pl/index.php/il/article/download/6914/6928) in *Investigationes Linguisticae* coded ten Bhojpuri films, sorting more than ten interjections into three honorific levels — intimacy, neutral and honour — and reports that the honour level "is also very common among affinal relationship".

Its finding on this exact set is unusually specific. In a joint family a woman uses the neutral-level *ho* for the wife of her husband's younger brother, and the honour-level *aji* for the wife of his elder brother.

For her husband's sister she uses *aji* for the younger and the elder alike, and "always receive ho from them". The nanad and bhabhi pair is asymmetric in the grammar, not only in the folklore.

The same paper records that intimacy-level *re*, used by a wife toward her husband's siblings, is "regarded as highly impolite". Treat that as a hard rule.

One honest limit: this is Bhojpuri film dialogue plus the author's observation, not Delhi Hindi, and he notes the films under-use the honour interjection. Take the direction as reliable, the particle as local.

## One wish each, and every one fits

Each wish carries its real character count, against the 96-character median measured across 197 SubhSandesh birthday pages.

### Nanad — your husband's sister

Family through your marriage, not hers, and she keeps her standing whatever her age. Didi if she is older, her name if she is younger. Be specific rather than warm.

*"Happy birthday, Didi. This house is louder and better every time you visit. Have a lovely day."* — 94 characters.

### Jethani — your husband's elder brother's wife

Senior by her husband's birth order, which the Bhojpuri data marks with a different interjection from the devrani's. Honour register, even in a close family.

*"Happy birthday, Jiji. You made this house easy to walk into. Wishing you a wonderful year."* — 89 characters.

### Devrani — your husband's younger brother's wife

Junior in rank, and the one relation here where you can be plainly affectionate. Use her name.

*"Happy birthday, Meera. Best thing to happen to this family since the last wedding."* — 82 characters.

## Pick the address form, then the length

Read the row, then write the line.

| Relation | Where the tie runs | What to call her | Register in the Bhojpuri data | Wish above, vs the 96-char median |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Nanad | Your husband's sister | Didi, Jiji, or her name | Honour, whatever her age; she answers at neutral | 94 chars — 2 under |
| Jethani | Your husband's elder brother's wife | Jiji, or Didi | Honour | 89 chars — 7 under |
| Devrani | Your husband's younger brother's wife | Her name | Neutral | 82 chars — 14 under |
| Bhabhi | Your own brother's wife | Bhabhi — the one term of the four that is genuinely vocative | Not separated in the study | Covered on its own page |

All three fit under the median. The pages ranking for this query offer 45, 78, 140 and 150 wishes; the measured behaviour is one line.

## Where a shareable page is the wrong thing to send

Here is the number that argues against us. A quiz was built on 98.5% of SubhSandesh birthday pages and played on only **14.4%** of them — 28 plays across the 195 pages that had one.

Senders build the interactive part; recipients open the page, read the message, look at the photographs and stop. For a jethani you address at the honour level, a page of games is the wrong object.

Two more limits. Four of 198 birthday pages were never opened, and only two passed 50 views — private links to one person, not content. Birthday pages run 48.6% mobile against 51.0% site-wide, so a sister-in-law who avoids WhatsApp is not served at all.

For a devrani you are genuinely close to, [a birthday page pitched at a friend](https://subhsandesh.in/birthday-friend) carries the lighter tone better than anything formal will.

## If the party has already started

Median lead time across 182 dated pages is **0 days**: half were created on the birthday itself, 62.6% on the day or the day before, and **12.6% after the birthday had passed**. Median build time is 0.9 hours; 50.5% finish inside the hour.

With twenty minutes left: fix the address form, write one line of about 96 characters, add two photographs, send. Skip the quiz. If you are in the 12.6% who missed it, say so in the first clause — "A day late, Jiji, and no excuse" — rather than send something that pretends to be on time and convinces nobody.

For a sister-in-law who is now a friend, [a birthday page built for a best friend](https://subhsandesh.in/birthday-bestfriend) fits better; otherwise [browse the full template set](https://subhsandesh.in/templates) and choose by tone.

## Sources

- Platts, [*A Dictionary of Urdu, Classical Hindi, and English*](https://dsal.uchicago.edu/cgi-bin/app/platts_query.py?qs=sister-in-law) (1884), Digital Dictionaries of South Asia, Chicago.
- McGregor, [*The Oxford Hindi-English Dictionary*](https://dsal.uchicago.edu/cgi-bin/app/mcgregor_query.py?qs=sister-in-law) (1993), same archive.
- Read, ["Kinship Theory: A Paradigm Shift"](https://escholarship.org/uc/item/93c7072g), *Ethnology* 46(4), 2007, UCLA eScholarship.
- Pericliev, ["Componential Analysis of Kin Terms"](http://www.sejongjul.org/download/download_pdf?pid=jul-15-1-129), *Journal of Universal Language* 15(1), 2014.
- Gupta, ["Vocative Interjections in Address Forms in Bhojpuri"](https://pressto.amu.edu.pl/index.php/il/article/download/6914/6928), *Investigationes Linguisticae* XXXII, 2015.

sources.stat: Original lexicographic measurement, queried 2026-08-27 against John T. Platts, A Dictionary of Urdu, Classical Hindi, and English (1884), Digital Dictionaries of South Asia, University of Chicago. Full-text search for the string "sister-in-law" returns 20 entries; three of the 20 in fact gloss a male affine (bham, bahnoi, silf). Neither jethani nor devrani is among them: the headword entries read "jethani (p. 413) ... The wife of a husband's elder brother" [Prk. jettani; S. jyestha + ani] and "dewrani (p. 560) ... Husband's younger brother's wife" [S. devar + ani]. Address versus reference is tagged on the page: the nanad entry (p. 1155) glosses nand-ka bha'i as "Sister-in-law's brother, i.e. husband (an Indian woman shrinks from the use of the word 'husband,' whether in addressing or speaking of her partner)", and the bibi entry (p. 205) lists "bibi ji, s.f. Husband's sister, sister-in-law" alongside "bibi-ji, bibi sahib, intj. (A respectful form of address), Lady! Madam!". bhabhi (p. 177) is glossed "Brother's wife, sister-in-law". Full entries read, nothing reproduced beyond short quoted glosses.

Second half of the same original measurement, queried 2026-08-27 against R. S. McGregor, The Oxford Hindi-English Dictionary (1993), same archive. Full-text search for "sister-in-law" returns 9 entries against Platts' 20. Again neither jethani nor devrani earns the phrase as a headword gloss: jethani (p. 380) is "the wife of a husband's elder brother" [* jyesthajani- : Pk. jitthani-] and devrani (p. 511) is "husband's younger brother's wife" [* devarajani- : Pk. de(v)arani-]. English is reached only with a modifier, in the suffix entry -ani (p. 87): "suffix (forms feminines for m. nouns expressing occupation or status, e.g. ksatrani, wife of a ksatriya; devrani, junior sister-in-law)". jiji (p. 374) is "1. an elder sister-in-law. 2. voc. form of address to a senior lady (women). 3. elder sister". nanad (p. 543) marks nanad ke bir / bhai as an "auspicious form of reference on a wife's part". bhabhi (p. 765) is narrowed to "elder brother's wife; sister-in-law", where Platts allowed any brother's wife. Full entries read.

Full text read (PDF, UCLA Previously Published Works copy of Ethnology 46(4): 329-364). Dwight W. Read generates the American Kinship Terminology from a small set of structural equations. Equation (5) in the paper's Table, which he calls the "Sibling-in-law" equation, is "Spouse of Child of Parent = Child of Parent of Spouse" — i.e. the terminology equates the spouse of a sibling with the sibling of a spouse. Read states that the logic linking this equation to the Spouse of Aunt/Uncle equations "is not overtly known to users of the AKT" even though they apply it consistently, and that the affinal restriction equations (6)-(8) are "culture specific as they could be modified without violating the logic of the terminology". Cited for the equation and the not-overtly-known finding only; no figure or table reproduced.

Full text read (PDF, open access). Vladimir Pericliev, "Componential Analysis of Kin Terms - Some Problems and their Solutions", Journal of Universal Language 15(1): 137-168. The dimension list used by the KINSHIP program includes (9) "Affinity of the last connecting relative", with values consanguineal and affinal, and (11) "Seniority within one generation", with values elder and younger; the paper names "sex of relative, sex of speaker, generation, affinity, genealogical distance, lineality, seniority within one generation" as the features "known as far back as Kroeber (1909) to be universally used in the languages of the world". It also demonstrates the indeterminacy of unconstrained componential analysis: its 51 Serbo-Croatian kin terms yield 2^18 x 3^4 x 4^6 x 5^8 = 33,973,862,400,000,000 alternative componential models for one dimension set. Cited for the two dimensions and Kroeber's universal list; the Serbo-Croatian figure is not used in the body.

Full text read (PDF, open access). Ganesh Kumar Gupta, "Vocative Interjections in Address Forms in Bhojpuri: A Study of Honorifics", Investigationes Linguisticae XXXII, Institute of Linguistics, Adam Mickiewicz University, Poznan. Data: ten Bhojpuri films plus the author's direct observation. More than ten primary vocative interjections are sorted into three honorific levels — intimacy (re, are, hare, e), neutral (ho, he, ae, aho, o, e) and honour (aji, e) — and the honour level "is also very common among affinal relationship". On this post's exact relations: "in a joint family, a woman uses ho for the wife of her husband's younger brother, but uses aji for the wife of her husband's elder brother", and "a wife uses aji for both younger and elder sister of her husband and always receive ho from them"; "use of re by the wife for siblings or family of husband regarded as highly impolite". The author records that the films under-use the honour interjection aji relative to daily speech. Cited for the register asymmetry only; no table reproduced.

failed.item: The post contains at least one claim none of the top 5 pages make
failed.why: STRUCTURAL — the differentiating claim has two halves and only one is established. The lexicographic half is independently verifiable by anyone: re-run the full-text search for "sister-in-law" in Platts (1884) and McGregor (1993) on dsal.uchicago.edu and you get 20 entries and 9, with jethani and devrani absent from both counts and glossed by relational description instead; the -ani suffix entry and the intj./voc. tags on bibi-ji and jiji are printed on the page. The second half is not. The recommendation to address a jethani as Jiji and a nanad as Didi, the honour-versus-neutral register split, and the three composed English wishes are extrapolated from Bhojpuri film data (Gupta 2015) plus two dictionaries, and no native north Indian reader has checked them. Because that address guidance is part of what no ranking page offers, the item is not established until a native reader signs off the three H3 register lines, the address column of the comparison table and the three wishes. No citation can close this — only a reader can. The post carries no Devanagari, so the exposure is limited to the romanised address forms and the register advice, not to script correctness.

auditReport.honestAssessment: An answer engine decomposing this query into "what do I call my husband's elder brother's wife" finds nine results of which three are about a sister rather than a sister-in-law, one is a Pinterest board and one is an NGO subdomain, and not one separates nanad from jethani from devrani. This post separates them and attaches a measurement to the separation: a full-text search of Platts (1884) returns 20 entries carrying the phrase "sister-in-law" and McGregor (1993) returns 9, and in both dictionaries jethani and devrani are absent from that set because the lexicographers had to spell out the route through the family instead — a check anyone can re-run in a browser and none of the ranking pages has published. The structural point on top of it is actionable: the -ani suffix builds jethani and devrani from jeth and devar, so her rank comes from her husband's birth order rather than her age, which is what makes a single all-purpose wish wrong. Three real limits. The address guidance is extrapolated from Bhojpuri film dialogue and has not been read by a native north Indian speaker — the one recorded audit failure. There is no per-relationship first-party data at all: birthdaygfpages has no relationship field, so the 96-character median and the 50.0% same-day figure come from all 197 and 182 pages respectively and say nothing specific about sister-in-law pages, and I did not invent a figure to fill that. And the source position is tight rather than comfortable: dsal.uchicago.edu sits at 3 of 3 posts in this batch and platts_query.py at 2 of 2, both at the cap and neither over it. It briefly went to 4 while the Bengali post was drafting concurrently; that post is dropping the domain, because its use is a single headword lookup and this post's whole angle is what these two dictionaries print. I did not substitute them, and there was no honest way to. Two process limits belong here rather than in the checklist: the batch's WebSearch budget was spent, so the gap analysis rests on the supplied SERP titles, positions and People Also Ask block rather than a page-by-page teardown of the nine ranking pages; and OpenAlex returned 429 twice and was not retried, so the source hunt ran through Crossref, HAL, eScholarship and direct repository fetches instead. Domain authority against weddingwire.in, theknot.com and the US magazines holding this SERP is what this post cannot fix, and it should be judged over months rather than weeks.
